name: PDRN / Polynucleotides
lead: Polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN) is a mixture of DNA fragments, typically 50 to 1,500 kDa in size, purified from salmon or trout sperm and originally isolated from human placenta in Italy [1][2]. It is used in injectable and topical "skin booster" or biorevitalisation treatments marketed for skin rejuvenation, scar improvement and recovery after procedures such as laser or microneedling, and it is widely used in Asia as a dermatological biostimulator [1][2][3].

Related products labelled polynucleotides (PN) are made of longer DNA chains; a 2025 review distinguishes them from PDRN, describing PN as acting mainly on extracellular matrix remodelling and PDRN as acting through adenosine receptor activation and nucleotide supply [4].

The best-established clinical evidence concerns wound healing, for example diabetic foot ulcers, rather than appearance. A 2025 systematic review of polynucleotides in aesthetic medicine found only nine studies of low to moderate quality covering 219 patients, with variation in injection techniques and products [5][6].

paras: Wikipedia describes PDRN as a mixture of single-stranded oligonucleotides, peaking around 350 kDa in some commercial forms, obtained by fractionating and purifying DNA from salmon or trout sperm. A purification step is described as removing proteins and peptides that might trigger immune reactions, giving a product of about 95 percent purity [1][2]. The 2017 Frontiers in Pharmacology review describes a proprietary registered drug derived from Oncorhynchus mykiss or Oncorhynchus keta DNA [6]. Alternative sources, including plant, microbial and human-derived material, are an active research area, and lower-molecular-weight fragments are reported to penetrate skin and enter cells more readily [1][2].

In aesthetic clinics, PDRN and polynucleotides are injected into the skin in "skin booster" or "salmon DNA" treatments aimed at texture, hydration, fine lines, acne scars and post-procedure recovery [3][5][7]. A 2025 randomised trial studied air-botulinum toxin combined with PDRN injections for acne scars [8]. A 2023 randomised trial examined early postoperative PDRN injections for hypertrophic scarring after thyroidectomy [9], and a 2026 narrative review covers its use for recovery after aesthetic procedures [10]. Reviews of cosmeceutical use discuss extraction methods and topical applications [11].

PDRN has been used in wound care and musculoskeletal medicine. A randomised double-blind trial in Italy tested it on chronic diabetic foot ulcers [12], a Korean randomised trial examined pressure ulcers [13], and trials have tested ultrasound-guided PDRN injection for rotator cuff tendinopathy and PDRN eye drops after photorefractive keratectomy [14][15]. ClinicalTrials.gov lists PDRN studies in diabetic ulcers, scleroderma, rotator cuff tears, epicondylitis, spinal stenosis and menopausal genitourinary symptoms [16][17][18][19][20].

For aesthetic skin use, a 2025 systematic review of polynucleotides identified nine studies of low to moderate quality (219 patients) and noted variation in injection areas and techniques [5]. A narrative review of salmon-DNA treatments for post-procedure recovery was published in 2026 [10].

Randomised trials exist for specific scar and wound uses. The 2025 air-botulinum toxin plus PDRN study for acne scars and the 2023 thyroidectomy scar trial are examples, and a phase 4 registered study examined PDRN in post-operative scars (22 participants) [8][9][21]. A 2026 registered phase 2 study compares fractional CO2 laser with and without PDRN for facial scars [22].

In wound healing, a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in two Italian centres evaluated PDRN for hard-to-heal diabetic foot ulcers, with a 215-participant study registered on ClinicalTrials.gov [12][16]. Wikipedia reports that studies in diabetic foot ulcers showed reduced healing time versus placebo [1].

The most commonly proposed mechanism is activation of adenosine A2A receptors after enzymatic degradation of the polymer to adenosine, raising cAMP and upregulating pathways such as PI3K/Akt and vascular endothelial growth factor, with additional supply of nucleotides to the salvage pathway [1][6][2]. Reviews describe anti-inflammatory effects through reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines and NF-kB signalling, and promotion of angiogenesis and collagen production [1][2][23]. Laboratory studies report PDRN effects on fibroblast senescence and on SIRT1 in skin-ageing models, and a 2008 study reported angiogenesis and wound healing in diabetic mice [24][25][26]. A 2025 review states that PN and PDRN differ in function because of polymer length [4].

A 2024 review states that in vivo tests and clinical trials have found PDRN non-toxic [11]. Injection carries general procedural risks such as bruising and infection, and because the material is fish-derived, allergy is a theoretical concern; reviews describe the purification process as aimed at reducing immunogenicity [1][6]. The systematic review of aesthetic polynucleotides noted the least side effects as a goal of the field but concluded evidence quality was limited [5].

PDRN was originally isolated from human placenta for pharmaceutical use in Italy and is now sourced largely from salmon or trout [1]. A Google Trends dataset published in 2026 documents public search interest in PDRN and polynucleotides from 2019 to 2026 [27]. Wikipedia states that its most common application in Asia is as a dermatological biostimulator after abrasive procedures [1].
